hints: Count the longest carbon chain containing the C=C double bond and number it so the double bond gets the lowest possible number.
walkthrough:
Find the parent chain and the double bond**
Look at Y, you have three carbons in a row with a double bond at one end: $\text{ClCH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$. The parent is propene, and if you number from the right, the double bond starts at carbon 1, so it is prop-1-ene.

Add the chloro substituent**
The $\text{Cl}$ is on the carbon furthest from the double bond, which is carbon 3 when numbered to give the double bond the lowest number. Combine this to give $\text{3-chloroprop-1-ene}$.

hints: Look at the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs around each carbon to decide if it is tetrahedral or trigonal planar.
Recall the standard bond angle for four single bonds around carbon compared with the angle around a C=C double bond.
walkthrough:
Sort out angle a**
Angle a is around the $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ carbon. That carbon has four single bonds and no lone pairs, so it has four bonding pairs arranged tetrahedrally to get as far apart as possible. The tetrahedral angle is $109.5^{\circ}$.

Sort out angle b**
Angle b is around the $\text{C=CH}_2$ carbon. Each carbon in a $\text{C=C}$ double bond has three regions of electron density and no lone pairs, giving a trigonal planar arrangement. The ideal trigonal planar angle is $120^{\circ}$.

hints: Count every carbon, hydrogen, chlorine and oxygen in the displayed structure of Z, remembering that each line end and bend is a carbon with enough hydrogens to make four bonds.
walkthrough:
Count atom by atom**
Z is $\text{ClCH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$. That gives 3 carbons, 2 oxygens and 1 chlorine. For hydrogens: $2$ on the $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, $1+1$ on the $\text{CH(OH)}$, $2+1$ on the $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, totalling $7$. So the molecular formula is $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{7}\text{ClO}_{2}$.

hints: Think about what cold, dilute, acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ does to a C=C bond compared with hot, concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-$.
walkthrough:
Recognise the change at the double bond**
Y has a $\text{C=C}$ bond and Z has two $\text{C-OH}$ groups in its place. Two oxygen atoms have been added across the double bond using cold, dilute $\text{MnO}_4^-$. Addition of oxygen is oxidation, here mild oxidation to form a diol.

hints: For each C-OH carbon in Z, count how many other carbons are directly attached to that carbon to decide primary (1), secondary (2) or tertiary (3).
walkthrough:
Classify each OH in turn**
The $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ carbon is joined to only one other carbon, so it is primary. The $\text{CH(OH)}$ carbon is joined to two other carbons ($\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), so it is secondary. There is no carbon joined to three other carbons, so no tertiary alcohol. Tick primary and secondary only.
Final answer: primary ✓ and secondary ✓ ticked; tertiary blank

hints: Look for a C=O double bond in each formula, remembering that a carboxylic acid also contains C=O but is not normally classed as a carbonyl compound in this test.
walkthrough:
Spot the C=O**
A is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$, a ketone with $\text{C=O}$. B is $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CHO}$, an aldehyde with $\text{C=O}$. C is an alcohol and D is a carboxylic acid, so only A and B contain the ketone or aldehyde carbonyl group.

hints: Start by sorting A to D into functional groups: ketone, aldehyde, alcohol, carboxylic acid.
Recall which single functional group gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent on gentle warming.
Recall the structural requirement for a positive iodoform test, the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group or the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$ group.
Check which of A ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$) and C ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) can be oxidised by alkaline iodine to that fragment.
Recall what colour precipitate confirms the iodoform reaction.
Think about which functional groups contain an O-H that is acidic enough to react with sodium metal.
Decide whether the ketone A or aldehyde B will react with sodium metal.
Recall the visible change when sodium reacts, gas evolution and disappearance of the metal.
walkthrough:
Label the four unknowns**
Keep this map in mind: A $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$ is a ketone, B $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CHO}$ is an aldehyde, C $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is a primary alcohol, D $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ is a carboxylic acid.

Tollens' reagent picks out the aldehyde**
Tollens' reagent, $\text{[Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$, is a mild oxidising agent that oxidises aldehydes but not ketones, alcohols or acids under these conditions. So only B reacts: $$\text{RCHO + 2[Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+ + 3OH^- \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2^- + 2\text{Ag + 4NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ You see a silver mirror coating the tube, also accepted as a grey, black, brown or silver precipitate.

Alkaline iodine picks out A and C**
The iodoform test is positive for methyl ketones ($\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$) and for ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ which is oxidised in situ to $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$). A is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$, it contains $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$, so positive. C is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, so positive. B is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ with no methyl carbonyl, and D has no such group, so both negative. The positive observation is a pale yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_3$.

Sodium metal picks out C and D**
Sodium reacts with any O-H group that can release $\text{H}_2$: alcohols and carboxylic acids. So C and D react: $$\text{2CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH + 2Na \rightarrow 2CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{ONa + H}_2$$ $$\text{2CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H + 2Na \rightarrow 2CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{Na + H}_2$$ A and B have no O-H, so no reaction. The observation is effervescence from $\text{H}_2$ gas, with the sodium disappearing.

Final answer: Tollens' reagent: B; silver mirror or grey/black/brown/silver precipitate
alkaline solution of iodine: A and C; pale yellow precipitate
sodium metal: C and D; effervescence
